title: Ending with dignity
hook: a divorce document, and a hope for kindness on both sides

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shalom bayit, and your line was peace at home. Today, the hard case: when a home can't hold its peace any longer.

A scribe dips a quill. Around the table sit a rabbinic court of three and two witnesses, and across from them, two people who once stood under a canopy together. The scribe writes a short document by hand, on purpose, for this one couple, their names spelled out with care. It is folded, then placed into her hands, and she takes it. That is all. No shouting, no verdict about who was right. Jewish law knows that some marriages end. The question it keeps asking is how.
screen: `A COURT OF THREE.` → `A DOCUMENT WRITTEN BY HAND.` → `PLACED INTO HER HANDS.`

segments.voice: The document is called a get, and its root is in the Torah. In Deuteronomy, the old Jewish Publication Society translation describes a husband who "writeth her a bill of divorcement, and giveth it in her hand." It is written. A divorce in Jewish law isn't a mood or a slammed door; it's a careful act before witnesses, so no one is left wondering whether they are free. Clarity is its own kind of kindness. It is given into a hand: the ending happens person to person. In traditional law the husband gives and the wife receives, and both must do it willingly. And the sorrow is allowed. The prophet Malachi has God say, "For I hate putting away." The Talmud adds a picture some readers never forget: when a man divorces the wife of his youth, even the altar sheds tears. Divorce is permitted, and it is still a loss worth grieving. Now the hard part, said plainly. Because the get must be given freely, a spouse can refuse to give it, and a woman can be left unable to remarry. She is called an agunah, a chained woman. Rabbis and communities have worked on this for a long time, and today some couples sign agreements before the wedding so that no one is ever trapped. Underneath it all is a hope: kindness on both sides, even at the end. A marriage that began with blessings can close with honesty, clear words, and no one humiliated.
screen: `IT IS WRITTEN.` · `GIVEN INTO A HAND.` · `EVEN THE ALTAR SHEDS TEARS.` · `NO ONE LEFT CHAINED.` · then, large: `END WITH DIGNITY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something in your life that is ending, or should: a job, a habit, a friendship that has run its course. Ask, a few breaths apart: is the ending clear, is it person to person rather than a vanishing act, and is there anything kind I could still say? Let one honest, gentle sentence form, and if you pray, hold the people on the other side of that ending in your prayer.
Ending with dignity. A get written by hand, given into a hand, a loss allowed to be a loss, and no one left chained. Today's word.
Your line: end with dignity. An ending can still be clear, and still be gentle. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In traditional Jewish law a marriage ends with a get, a divorce document written by a scribe and given by the husband to the wife before a rabbinic court and witnesses; some couples today also sign a prenuptial agreement meant to ensure a get is never withheld.

chat.says: Does Jewish law even allow divorce? I thought marriage was meant to be forever.
options: Yes, by a written get given before witnesses; allowed, though still grieved as a loss.
No, Jewish law forbids divorce; unhappy couples can only separate and live apart.
Yes, and either spouse can end it alone, just by saying so out loud.
chat.meaning: Jewish law permits divorce through a get, written and given into a hand before witnesses; Malachi and the Talmud still treat it as a loss.

notes: Deuteronomy 24:1 and Malachi 2:16 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording.
Gittin 90b (the altar sheds tears over one who divorces his first wife) paraphrased; confirm.
Hook describes a beit din of three, a scribe, two witnesses; confirm this is a fair general description across communities.

'Both must do it willingly' reflects the later rule (attributed to Rabbeinu Gershom) that a wife cannot be divorced against her will, alongside the requirement that the husband give freely; Keeper to confirm the phrasing and source line (Yevamot 112b is approximate).
Agunah and prenuptial agreements: kept general ('some couples'); confirm fair across Orthodox and liberal communities. Reform practice differs on requiring a get; Keeper may want a line.
